title: R is 1.5. Does the outbreak take off?
hook: Each case infects 1.5 others on average. Is one arriving case sure to start an epidemic?

knows: R above 1 means an outbreak grows on average (immunity-eats-r)
R is the average number of people one case infects
doesNotKnow: that with R = 1.5 (Poisson spread), about 42% of single introductions die out by chance

misconception: If R is above 1, every introduced case starts an epidemic.
objective: The learner can explain that with Poisson spread and R = 1.5 about 42% of single introductions die out by chance, because the first cases often infect 0 or 1 people (56% of the time), so R above 1 makes growth possible, not certain.

claims.text: With Poisson spread and mean 1.5, the chance that one case's chain dies out is 41.7%.
claims.source: Extinction probability q is the smallest solution of q = e^{R(q − 1)} (probability generating function of the Poisson distribution). Builder's fixed-point iteration from q = 0 (scratchpad ncmc/outbreak.mjs), 2026-10-14: R = 1.5 gives 0.4172. Matches brief life.health-epidemiology NCM #1.

claims.text: The chance is about 20% for R = 2 and about 6% for R = 3; for R below 1 every chain dies out.
claims.source: Same fixed point: R = 2 gives 0.2032, R = 3 gives 0.0595, R = 0.9 gives 1 (for R ≤ 1 the only solution in [0, 1] is q = 1). Builder's node run, scratchpad ncmc/outbreak.mjs, 2026-10-14.

claims.text: In the stage's seeded run at R = 1.5, 38 of the first 101 outbreaks die out and 418 of 1,000; the reveal quotes the learner's own tally.
claims.source: Demo.tsx outbreak(): Poisson offspring by Knuth's product method, mulberry32 seed 218 + 10R (233 at R = 1.5), one stream per R; a chain passing 2,000 cases counts as taking off. Builder's node mirror of the same code (scratchpad ncmc/outbreak.mjs), 2026-10-14: at R = 1.5, after 1 outbreak 0 died (outbreak 1 took off), after 100 37 died, after 101 38, after 1,000 418 (41.8%). At R = 0.9 all 1,000 died; R = 2 237 of 1,000; R = 3 48 of 1,000. The seed formula reuses the brief's seed 218 and was not chosen for its result; the brief's own run (seed 218, 10,000 chains) gave 42.9%.

claims.text: With Poisson spread and mean 1.5, a case infects 0 or 1 others 56% of the time, so a chain often starts too thin to survive bad luck.
claims.source: P(0) + P(1) = e^{-1.5}(1 + 1.5) = 0.5578. Stage tally 'First case infected 0 or 1' in the seeded run: 49 of 101 and 547 of 1,000 at R = 1.5 (scratchpad ncmc/outbreak.mjs).

claims.text: R above 1 means growth is possible, not certain: a single introduction can die out by chance.
claims.source: Branching-process view of early epidemics: Easley & Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 21 (branching process model of epidemics). Attribution for the fact-checker to confirm; follows from c1.

claims.text: This assumes Poisson spread, with every case equally infectious; real spread is more uneven, which makes dying out even more likely.
claims.source: Lloyd-Smith J.O., Schreiber S.J., Kopp P.E. & Getz W.M. (2005), 'Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence', Nature 438:355-359: for a fixed R, more individual variation (smaller negative-binomial k) raises the probability that an introduction goes extinct. Required by the brief's acceptance edit; the existing lesson spreaders-are-rare cites the same paper.

claims.text: Each R has its own seeded run; an outbreak passing 2,000 cases is counted as taking off.
claims.source: Stage set-up (Demo.tsx seedFor, CAP), from the brief's check.

recall.question: A disease with R = 2 reaches a new town through one case. What is most likely?
options: It usually spreads, but there is a real chance (about 1 in 5) it dies out by itself
It is certain to spread, because R is above 1
It almost always dies out, because one case is too few
recall.why: R above 1 makes growth possible, not certain. Early on there are only a few cases, and each may infect nobody by chance; with Poisson spread and R = 2 about 20% of single introductions fizzle.
